beats.headline: Why does your deployment cause 502 errors?
beats.subline: It is a race condition between Kubernetes and your Spring Boot lifecycle.
beats.narration: Kubernetes rolling updates are rarely enough for zero-downtime. If your app shuts down while traffic is still hitting it, your users get 502s. Let's fix that.

beats.title: Blue-Green Traffic Flow
beats.subtitle: Switching traffic via Service selectors
beats.narration: Blue-Green runs two identical environments. You verify Green while Blue handles traffic. Once ready, you flip the Service selector to Green. It is fast, but risky if your database isn't backward compatible.

beats.title: Instant Traffic Cutover
beats.caption: Atomic selector patch

lines.text: # Flip traffic from Blue to Green
# Instant rollback if things go south

beats.narration: The secret is patching the Service selector. It's an atomic operation. If Green fails, flip back to Blue instantly. Just keep Blue warm for 30 minutes before scaling to zero.

beats.title: Blue-Green vs. Rolling Update
beats.narration: Rolling updates are low-cost but slow to revert. Blue-Green costs double the compute but offers the safest rollback path. Choose based on your tolerance for downtime.

beats.title: Blue-Green Locked In
takeaways: Use Service selectors for atomic cutovers
Keep old environment warm for rollbacks
Beware of shared state deserialization bugs

beats.headline: What if you only want to expose 5% of users?
beats.subline: Stop flipping 100% of traffic at once. Use progressive delivery.
beats.narration: Blue-Green is binary. Canary is surgical. We shift 5% of traffic to the new version, verify metrics, and only then proceed. This is how you stop bugs before they hit everyone.

beats.title: Canary Traffic Split
beats.subtitle: Managed by Istio + Argo
beats.narration: Istio handles the L7 traffic weight. Argo Rollouts monitors Prometheus metrics. If the canary error rate spikes, Argo automatically resets the weight to zero. No human intervention required.

beats.title: Argo Rollout Strategy
beats.code:
strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
    - setWeight: 5
    - pause: { duration: 5m }
    - analysis:
        templates: [{name: canary-check}]

steps.explanation: Start with 5% traffic to minimize blast radius.

beats.narration: This configuration tells Argo to shift 5 percent, wait 5 minutes, and run an analysis. If the analysis fails, the rollout aborts. It's the ultimate safety net for production.

beats.title: Isolating Canary Metrics
beats.caption: Crucial: filter by pod template hash
beats.narration: Never use service-wide metrics for canary analysis. If you do, the 95 percent of healthy stable traffic will hide the canary's errors. Always filter by the pod template hash.

beats.title: Canary Delivery Locked In
takeaways: Use Istio for L7 traffic splitting
Filter metrics by pod template hash

beats.headline: One column rename can kill your production app.
beats.subline: Don't break your schema while v1 pods are still running.
beats.narration: Database changes are the hardest part of zero-downtime. If you rename a column, your old pods will crash. You need the Expand and Contract pattern.

beats.title: Expand and Contract Phases
beats.subtitle: Safe schema evolution
beats.narration: First, expand the schema by adding a nullable column. Second, dual-write from your code. Third, backfill the data. Finally, contract by dropping the old column once v1 is dead.

beats.title: Dual-Write Strategy

steps.explanation: Write to both columns so v1 and v2 stay in sync.
Read from new column, fallback to old if null.

beats.narration: Your code acts as the bridge. Write to both columns during the transition. Use a getter to fallback to the legacy column if the new one is empty. This keeps both versions happy.

beats.title: Throttled Backfill
beats.caption: Avoid locking the table!

lines.text: UPDATE customers SET full_name = name WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE full_name IS NULL LIMIT 5000);

beats.narration: Never run one giant update. It will lock your table and cause downtime. Use small, throttled batches with pauses in between to keep the database responsive.

beats.title: DB Migrations Locked In
takeaways: Use Expand and Contract for schema changes

beats.headline: Why does Kubernetes kill your pods too early?
beats.subline: The race between SIGTERM and your proxy routing table.
beats.narration: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM at the same time it updates routing tables. Your app dies before the proxy stops sending traffic. Here is how to force a clean handoff.

beats.title: Graceful Shutdown Sequence
beats.subtitle: Aligning K8s and Spring Boot
beats.narration: Add a preStop hook to sleep for 10 seconds. This gives the load balancer time to remove the pod from the routing table. Then, Spring Boot handles the graceful shutdown of active requests.

beats.title: Spring Boot Config
beats.code:
server:
  shutdown: graceful

spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s

steps.explanation: Wait 30s for active requests to finish.

beats.narration: Enable graceful shutdown in your YAML. Spring will stop accepting new requests but will wait up to 30 seconds for existing ones to finish. This is non-negotiable for production.

beats.title: Pod Spec Alignment
beats.caption: The math: preStop + Spring Timeout < GracePeriod
beats.narration: The math is simple. Your grace period must be longer than your sleep hook plus your Spring timeout. If you don't set this, Kubernetes will SIGKILL your app, cutting off active requests.

beats.title: Zero-Downtime Mastery Complete
takeaways: Use preStop hooks to drain traffic
